questions.prompt: In the negative-feedback block diagram, the summing junction forms the error signal \(s_{err}\). Which expression gives it?
questions.explanation:
The feedback block \(f\) takes a fraction of the output, \(f\,s_{out}\), and the junction SUBTRACTS it from the input (that is what 'negative' feedback means): \(s_{err}=s_{in}-f\,s_{out}\).
• Adding \(f\,s_{out}\) would be positive feedback.
• \(G\) multiplies the error afterwards; it is not part of the subtraction.
• Dividing by \(f\) mixes up which direction the signal travels in the loop.

questions.prompt: A feedback system has forward gain \(G\) and feedback factor \(f\). When \(Gf \gg 1\), the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+Gf)\) approaches
questions.explanation:
If \(Gf\gg1\) then \(1+Gf\approx Gf\), so \(\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}\approx\dfrac{G}{Gf}=\dfrac1f\). The gain is set by the feedback network alone, so even a sloppy, drifting \(G\) gives a precise closed-loop gain.
• Closed-loop gain \(\approx G\) would only happen if \(Gf\ll1\) (almost no feedback).
• \(Gf\) is the gain around the loop, not the gain from input to output.

questions.prompt: A feedback system has forward gain \(G=1000\) and feedback factor \(f=0.1\). What is the closed-loop gain \(s_{out}/s_{in}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{1000}{1+1000\cdot0.1}=\dfrac{1000}{101}=9.901\).
Compare with the shortcut \(1/f=10\): since \(Gf=100\gg1\), the shortcut is within 1%. Common mistake: forgetting the 1 in the denominator and answering \(G/(Gf)=10\) exactly.

questions.prompt: A temperature control loop has forward gain \(G=40\) (°C per unit of command) and a sensor in the feedback path with \(f=0.5\) (units per °C). What is the closed-loop gain from setpoint command to temperature, in °C per unit?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{40}{1+20}=1.90\). The ideal value \(1/f=2\) is off by \(1/(1+Gf)=4.8\%\) because the loop gain of 20 is only moderate.
• 40 ignores the feedback.
• 2 is the infinite-loop-gain limit.
• \(40/(1+0.5)=26.7\) adds f instead of the loop gain \(Gf\).

questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop (\(f=1\)) has forward gain \(G=200\). The input is a constant 3. What is the size of the error signal \(e=x-fy\) at the summing junction after settling?
questions.explanation:
\(e=\dfrac{x}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{3}{201}=0.0149\). The output is \(Ge=2.985\), almost equal to the input. A large loop gain drives the error close to zero, but never exactly to zero with finite G.
• 3 is the error with no feedback.
• \(3/200=0.015\) is close but uses G instead of \(1+Gf\).
• 0 would require infinite gain or an integrator.

questions.prompt: In a feedback system with \(f=0.05\), the forward gain \(G\) drops by 10%, from 1000 to 900 (aging or temperature). About how much does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.explanation:
Compute both: \(1000/(1+50)=19.61\) and \(900/(1+45)=19.57\). The change is \(0.22\%\).
In general \(\dfrac{dG_{cl}}{G_{cl}}=\dfrac{1}{1+Gf}\dfrac{dG}{G}\): feedback shrinks the sensitivity to \(G\) by the factor \(1+Gf\approx 50\), and \(10\%/50 = 0.2\%\). That is exactly why feedback is used for precision.
• 10% would be the no-feedback behavior.
• 5% and 2% don't match the factor \(1+Gf\approx50\).

questions.prompt: As \(G\to\infty\), the error signal \(s_{err}=s_{in}/(1+Gf)\) of a negative-feedback loop goes to zero, yet the output \(s_{out}\) stays finite and equal to \(s_{in}/f\). How is that consistent?
options: The output must also go to zero, since \(s_{out}=G\,s_{err}\) and \(s_{err}\to0\)
\(s_{out}=G\,s_{err}\): a vanishing \(s_{err}\) times an enormous \(G\) leaves a finite product, \(s_{in}/f\)
The loop breaks, so the output is undefined for infinite \(G\)
\(s_{err}\) is exactly zero for any finite \(G\), so the output is exactly \(s_{in}/f\) even for small \(G\)
questions.explanation:
\(s_{err}=s_{in}/(1+Gf)\) is never exactly zero for finite \(G\); it shrinks as \(1/G\). The output is \(G\cdot s_{err}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}s_{in}\to\dfrac{s_{in}}{f}\).
This is the origin of the 'golden rules' for op-amps: the input difference is ≈ 0 BECAUSE the gain is huge, while the output is whatever value makes the feedback signal \(f\,s_{out}\) equal \(s_{in}\). This is a '\(0\cdot\infty\)' limit.
• \(s_{out}\) cannot vanish: if it did, the feedback signal would be zero and the error would equal \(s_{in}\), contradicting \(s_{err}\to0\).
• The loop is perfectly well defined; the equation \(s_{out}=G(s_{in}-f s_{out})\) simply solves algebraically.

questions.prompt: A designer accidentally makes the feedback POSITIVE: \(s_{err}=s_{in}+f\,s_{out}\). The loop gain is \(Gf=0.9\) with \(G=50\). What is the closed-loop gain \(G/(1-Gf)\)?
options: 500, ten times larger than \(G\), and very sensitive to small changes in \(Gf\)
Infinite, because positive feedback always blows up
questions.explanation:
With positive feedback each trip around the loop adds a copy of the output: \(G_{closed}=G(1+T+T^2+\dots)=\dfrac{G}{1-T}\) for \(|T|<1\). Here \(T=0.9\), so \(G_{closed}=50/0.1=500\).
It is only infinite when \(T=1\) exactly, and it is hypersensitive near there: change \(T\) from 0.9 to 0.95 and the gain doubles to 1000. If \(T>1\) the output grows until something saturates ('railing out').
• \(50/(1+0.9)=26.3\) is the NEGATIVE-feedback answer.
• 'Always blows up' is false for \(T<1\).

questions.prompt: A designer wants the closed-loop gain to be within 0.1% of the ideal value \(1/f\), i.e. \(G_{closed}\ge 0.999/f\). What is the minimum loop gain \(T=Gf\) needed?
questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}\cdot f=\dfrac{Gf}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{T}{1+T}\). Setting \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=0.999\) gives \(T=\dfrac{0.999}{0.001}=999\).
So the loop gain must be about 1000 for 0.1% accuracy: the fractional error is \(\dfrac{1}{1+T}\). Common mistake: using \(T\ge0.999\).

questions.prompt: Preview of control-system concepts. In a room thermostat, the forward block is 'heater plus room' and the feedback block is the thermometer. With a large loop gain, the room settles near setpoint\(/f\). If the thermometer reads 2% high (f is 2% too large), what happens?
options: Nothing: feedback cancels sensor errors as well
The room settles about 2% below the intended temperature, because the loop trusts the sensor
The room settles about 2% above the intended temperature
questions.explanation:
With large loop gain the closed-loop gain is about \(1/f\), set by the feedback path. Feedback corrects errors inside the loop (plant drift, disturbances) but faithfully follows a biased measurement: a sensor reading 2% high makes the loop hold the true temperature about 2% low. This is why sensor accuracy matters more than actuator accuracy.
• Sensor errors sit in the feedback path, which is the one part feedback cannot correct.
• The direction is opposite: reading high means it stops heating too early.
• A 2% gain change does not affect stability here.

questions.prompt: Preview of noise rejection. A disturbance of size 10 (for example a load change or a sensor offset) is injected at the forward block's OUTPUT, as in the figure, with \(s_{in}=0\). The loop has \(G=1000\) and \(f=0.05\). How large is the disturbance's contribution to \(s_{out}\)?
questions.explanation:
With \(s_{in}=0\) and an additive disturbance, \(s_{out}=G(0-f\,s_{out})+s_{noise}\), so \(s_{out}=\dfrac{s_{noise}}{1+Gf}\).
Here \(Gf=50\), so \(s_{out}=\dfrac{10}{51}=0.196\). The loop 'sees' the disturbance as an error and fights it, rejecting it by the factor \(1+T\). Later skills (sensitivity and disturbance rejection) build on this.

questions.prompt: Preview of bandwidth extension. The forward amplifier is \(G(s)=\dfrac{1000}{1+j\omega/\omega_p}\) with \(f_p=\omega_p/2\pi=1\ \mathrm{kHz}\), used inside a negative-feedback loop with \(f=0.1\). The closed-loop transfer function has the same one-pole form. Where is its pole, in kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{G_0/(1+j\omega/\omega_p)}{1+G_0f/(1+j\omega/\omega_p)}=\dfrac{G_0}{(1+j\omega/\omega_p)+G_0f}=\dfrac{G_0/(1+T_0)}{1+j\omega/[\omega_p(1+T_0)]}\) with \(T_0=G_0f=100\).
The pole moves up by the factor \(1+T_0=101\): \(f_{p,closed}=1\ \mathrm{kHz}\times101=101\ \mathrm{kHz}\). The DC gain dropped by the same factor (1000 → 9.9), so feedback trades gain for bandwidth, the idea behind the gain-bandwidth product.
